introduction.text: The Basilica costantiniana di S. Agnese, also known as Santa Costanza, is a Roman mausoleum-turned-church located just outside Rome's ancient walls. It is one of the best preserved examples of Late Antique architecture and contains some of the finest surviving mosaics from the 4th century, making it a key monument for understanding early Christian art and imperial funerary practices.

history.description: Construction of the Constantinian basilica (funerary hall) began in 338 AD under Emperor Constantine I.
The mausoleum of Constantina was built around 350 AD, adjacent to the earlier basilica.
Constantina died in 354 AD, and her sarcophagus was placed in the mausoleum.
Pope Nicholas I celebrated mass in the building in 865 AD, the first recorded use of the name Santa Costanza.
The building was consecrated as a church in 1254 by Pope Alexander IV.
Excavations in 1992 uncovered an earlier building beneath the mausoleum, providing evidence of its early use.

design.description: Santa Costanza is a circular, centralized structure with an ambulatory surrounding a shallow central dome on a drum, supported by twelve pairs of granite columns and twelve clerestory windows, creating a contrast between light and dark spaces.

art.description: The building houses well-preserved 4th‑century mosaics in the ambulatory and apses, featuring secular motifs such as vines, grapes, and cupids, as well as early Christian iconography like Christ Pantocrator and the Traditio Legis.
